clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant Stickler syndrome caused by mutations in COL11A1, encoding the alpha-1 chain of type XI collagen.
The beaded congenital vitreous anomaly is characteristic of type 2, contrasting with the membranous vitreous of type 1.
Sensorineural hearing loss tends to be more frequent and more pronounced than in type 1.
High myopia with retinal detachment risk, the Pierre Robin sequence, midface hypoplasia and cleft palate are shared with type 1.
It is allelic with, and clinically overlaps, Marshall syndrome (also COL11A1), which shows more striking facial and ectodermal features.
It must be distinguished from COL11A2-related Stickler syndrome (type 3), which spares the eye because the alpha-2 chain of type XI collagen is not expressed in vitreous.
Type XI collagen co-assembles with type II collagen to regulate fibril diameter, explaining the overlap in systemic features with type 1.
Lifelong retinal surveillance and regular audiology are required.
reference.pathophysiology: Stickler syndrome type 2 is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in COL11A1, the gene for the alpha-1 chain of type XI collagen, a quantitatively minor fibrillar collagen that nucleates and co-polymerises with type II collagen to control the diameter and spacing of cartilage and vitreous fibrils. Pathogenic variants — frequently splice-site or in-frame changes acting through a dominant-negative mechanism — disrupt the type II/XI heterofibrillar network, degrading the architecture of the vitreous (producing the beaded vitreous anomaly and predisposing to giant retinal tears and detachment) and of cartilage (epiphyseal dysplasia, early osteoarthritis and craniofacial underdevelopment with the Robin sequence). Because type XI collagen is also important in the cochlea, sensorineural hearing loss is characteristically more prominent than in the COL2A1-related type 1. The same gene underlies Marshall syndrome, and the two conditions form an overlapping clinical spectrum.
additionalInvestigations: Dilated fundoscopy and slit-lamp examination with vitreous phenotyping (beaded anomaly) and refraction
Audiometry, with monitoring for progressive hearing loss
Cleft palate and airway assessment in infancy
redFlags: Symptoms of retinal detachment — flashes, floaters, a curtain-like field defect or sudden visual loss
Neonatal airway obstruction from the Robin sequence
reference.prognosis: Lifespan is normal; retinal detachment is the chief sight-threatening complication and hearing loss is often significant, but structured ophthalmic and audiological surveillance with timely intervention gives a good functional outlook.
pitfalls: Assuming COL11A2-related (type 3) disease involves the eye — it does not
Difficulty separating type 2 from allelic Marshall syndrome
Relying on systemic features alone without vitreous phenotyping to distinguish from type 1
Underestimating the degree and progression of hearing loss
references: Stickler syndrome surveillance and management guidance
management: Prophylactic retinopexy and urgent surgical repair of giant retinal tears and detachment
Lifelong ophthalmic surveillance with refractive correction of high myopia and detachment safety-netting
Close audiological monitoring and hearing amplification, as sensorineural loss is often more marked and progressive than in type 1
Manage early-onset osteoarthritis and epiphyseal dysplasia with analgesia, physiotherapy and joint protection
Cleft palate repair and airway management for Pierre Robin sequence in infancy
Genetic counselling and cascade family screening for the autosomal dominant COL11A1 variant, noting overlap with Marshall syndrome
Multidisciplinary care across ophthalmology, audiology, clinical genetics and orthopaedics
